title: The moon in exile
translation: If something terrible happens and you're drowning in grief, don't rush off and become a monk on an impulse. Better to quietly shut your gate, as if you barely existed, and let the days go by without expecting anything. There's something right about that.
Akimoto once said he'd like "to see the moon of exile without having done anything wrong". I know what he meant.
original: {不幸|ふかう}に{憂|うれ}へに{沈|しづ}める{人|ひと}の、{頭|かしら}おろしなど、ふつつかに{思|おも}ひとりたるにはあらで、{有|あ}るか{無|な}きかに{門|かど}さしこめて、{待|ま}つこともなく{明|あか}し{暮|く}らしたる、さるかたにあらまほし。
{顕基|あきもと}{中納言|ちゆうなごん}のいひけむ、「{配所|はいしよ}の{月|つき}、{罪|つみ}なくて{見|み}む。」こと、さもおぼえぬべし。
literal: A person sunk in grief through misfortune not deciding rashly to shave their head or the like, but shutting the gate as if barely existing, and passing the days and nights without waiting for anything: in its way, that is desirable.
What Middle Counsellor Akimoto is said to have said, 'I would like to see the moon of a place of exile without guilt': one can surely feel that way.

notes.text: 'Taking down the head': shaving the head, that is, taking vows as a Buddhist monk or nun. A common reaction to grief at the time.
'Rashly, crudely'. Modern {不束|ふつつか} means 'clumsy, inexperienced', as in the humble wedding phrase {不束者|ふつつかもの}ですが.
Minamoto no Akimoto (1000–1047), a court noble. When the emperor he served died, he left court and became a monk.

notes.quote: 配所の月、罪なくて見む
notes.text: Exile was a common punishment for courtiers, and the moon seen from a lonely place of exile was a classic subject of poetry. Akimoto wants the loneliness and the beauty without the crime. Kenkō likes that: withdrawal without drama.
